newsitem.title: UK: British Airways strike continues, dispute heats up.
newsitem.headline: British Airways strike continues, dispute heats up.

text.p: British Airways Plc said Thursday it expected to add to the number of flights it was operating, as a planned 72-hour strike by cabin crew entered its second day.
"We expect to run 20 percent more flights today and another 20 percent more tomorrow (the last day of the strike)," airline spokesman David Budgen said.
On Wednesday, the airline was forced to cancel between 20 percent and 30 percent of the 1,000 flights it operates worldwide each day, leaving 25,000 passengers stranded.
At London's Heathrow airport, which has borne the brunt of the strike, the airline expected to operate 53 percent of its normal long-haul flights Thursday.
At London Gatwick airport, the airline said it was running half of its long-haul services.
In a move to put pressure on the striking workers, the airline said it had 500 new recruits ready to come in to replace striking workers, with another 3,000 job applicants in the pipeline.

The airline has threatened to take legal action against the strikers. BA claims the 72-hour strike, which is set to continue until Saturday morning, is illegal because of a discrepancy in the strike ballot. The airline says more cabin crew voted on the strike ballot than were actually on the company payroll.

The strike is being held over a new pay structure the airline has implemented as part of a massive cost-saving drive, in which it hopes to slash 42 million pounds ($70.8 million) from its operating budget
George Ryde, the Transport & General Workers union's senior aviation official, said the union believed its ballot was legal and would be upheld in court if challenged.

The airline said 189 cabin crew had so far gone on strike, while 1,000 cabin crew had reported for work. Another 1,549 cabin crew had reported in sick, of which 163 had called in to say they would not be coming in to work, rather than admit they were striking for fear of reprisals from the airline.
Under U.K. aviation rules, airlines need 1 staff member for every 50 passengers.

Management has warned that employees face loss of travel perks and promotion opportunities if they went on strike. It has also threatened to dismiss or even sue individual strikers -- tactics the unions have termed "intimidatory" and "macho."

The industrial action is part of a war the airline is fighting on several fronts. The carrier is striving to get clearance for a massive alliance with American Airlines and is also fighting a legal challenge from Laker Airway Inc. in Florida.
